headline: Trump sued the BBC. Now a judge says: answer questions.
summary: Trump is suing the BBC for $10 billion over a documentary that spliced his January 6 speech. A federal magistrate judge in Miami ordered him on Thursday to sit for a deposition by December 11 or risk sanctions up to dismissal. He skipped an agreed date on October 16, citing national matters. The BBC says he was at a rally in Georgia.

cover_question.q: If you sue, do you have to testify?

cover_answer: Yes. The one who brings the case answers questions too.
table_question: If you start an argument, do you have to answer questions too?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president is suing a TV company in Britain called the BBC. He says a show cut up his words to make him sound worse than he meant. A judge said that if he wants the fight, he has to sit down and answer the other side's questions, like both players telling the referee what happened. That is how courts work, and it is the grown-ups' job.
5-7.why: A fight, a referee, both players answer. The courtroom is a rule they already know.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reads a story through one rule they already know, so the script makes this one the referee: if you want the call, you answer the referee's questions. The $10 billion and January 6 stay out. Expect "did the TV people lie?" They say they made a mistake and said sorry. The court decides the rest.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Last December Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion over a documentary that spliced his January 6 speech. In a lawsuit both sides get questioned under oath. He missed his turn on October 16, so a judge set December 11. Miss that and the case can be thrown out: a forfeit for a no-show.
8-12.why: Sue, get questioned, miss your turn, forfeit.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether rules bind the powerful the same as everyone else, and the script hands them one chain to test it on: sue, get questioned, miss your turn, risk forfeit. The forfeit is a mechanism they know from sport. Expect "can a president be forced?" The judge says yes, by December 11, or the case can go.

13-17.script: If you sue someone, should you be able to dodge their questions? Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion over a spliced January 6 clip; the BBC apologized for the edit but denies defamation. He skipped a deposition on October 16 and was at a rally in Georgia. Second: does the apology settle it, or does the jury?
13-17.why: Apology and lawsuit, both real. Which should count?
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the BBC admits the edit was wrong, and Trump may still lose the case he brought. The script asks them to weigh an apology against a trial, and to notice that the excuse and the rally are both on the record. Expect "so who's right?" Both can be partly right. That is what the jury is for.

5-7.a: When someone asks a court to settle a fight. A judge makes sure both sides play fair.

8-12.a: Questions under oath before the trial. Both sides do it.

8-12.q: Can he just not show up?
8-12.a: He skipped once. Skip December 11 and the case can be thrown out.

13-17.q: If you sue, do you have to testify?
13-17.a: Yes. The one who brings the case answers questions too.

13-17.q: Didn't the BBC admit it was wrong?
13-17.a: It apologized for the edit and two bosses resigned. It still denies defaming him.
